title: Hydrocarbons
overview: Understand the structure of benzene and its characteristic electrophilic substitution reactions. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Describe benzene and methylbenzene reactions with reagents and conditions.
Explain electrophilic substitution mechanisms for nitration and halogenation.
Compare ring substitution with side-chain reactions.

definitions.definition: An electron-pair acceptor attracted to electron-rich regions.
A reaction replacing a ring hydrogen by an electrophile while restoring aromaticity.
Extra stability from π-electron delocalisation around the ring.
Ring substitution introducing an alkyl group using a halogenoalkane and AlCl₃.
Ring substitution introducing an acyl group using an acyl chloride and AlCl₃.
A substituent influencing the positions favoured by further ring substitution.

sections.title: Core arene reactions
content: Benzene reacts with Br₂/AlBr₃ or Cl₂/AlCl₃, concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ at about 25–60 °C, CH₃Cl/AlCl₃ with heat, or CH₃COCl/AlCl₃ with heat. Hydrogenation uses H₂ with Ni/Pt and heat. Learn product, reagent, catalyst and condition as one package.
bullets: Bromine water alone does not rapidly decolourise benzene.
Friedel–Crafts products retain the aromatic ring.

sections.title: Electrophilic substitution mechanism
content: Generate the electrophile (for nitration, NO₂⁺). A curly arrow moves from the benzene π system to the electrophile, producing a positively charged intermediate; a base removes H⁺ and the C–H bond electrons restore delocalisation.
bullets: Curly arrows begin at an electron pair or bond.
Show the positive intermediate and restored ring.

sections.title: Methylbenzene and side chains
content: Methylbenzene can undergo ring substitution more readily than benzene, side-chain radical halogenation under UV light, and complete side-chain oxidation with hot alkaline KMnO₄ followed by acid to benzoic acid, provided a benzylic hydrogen is present.
bullets: Conditions decide ring versus side-chain halogenation.
Oxidation shortens an oxidisable alkyl side chain to –COOH.

sections.title: Directing effects
content: –NH₂, –OH and alkyl groups direct mainly to 2/4 positions; –NO₂, –COOH and –COR direct mainly to position 3. Use the substituent already on the ring to predict major isomers without claiming a single exclusive product.
bullets: Number positions relative to the existing substituent.
Directing effect and activation are related but not identical statements.

formulas.label: Side-chain oxidation
formulas.note: Hot alkaline KMnO₄, then dilute acid; requires a benzylic H.

examTips: For every organic reaction, revise reagent, condition, product and mechanism type together.
Place curly-arrow tails exactly at the bond or lone pair supplying electrons.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Drawing electrophilic addition instead of substitution.
Using bromine water without a halogen carrier for benzene ring bromination.
Ignoring reaction conditions when choosing ring versus side-chain substitution.

quickRecall.question: Why does benzene favour substitution over addition?
quickRecall.answer: Substitution restores aromatic delocalisation; addition would permanently lose that stabilisation.

quickRecall.question: What is the electrophile in nitration?
How do –OH and –NO₂ direct further substitution?
What conditions favour side-chain chlorination of methylbenzene?
quickRecall.answer: Chlorine with UV light/free-radical conditions rather than AlCl₃ ring-substitution conditions.
